cards.text: This psalm comes from the sons of Korah, written for the choirmaster. And friend, it does NOT ease you in. No warm-up, no soft intro, just a call to clap your hands and shout to God.

cards.question: The psalm opens with a call to clap and shout to God. Who does it call on to do it?

cards.text: And this is not polite little golf clapping, friend, this is shouting to God with a voice of triumph. Then the next line says how awesome the LORD Most High is.

cards.question: The psalm calls the LORD Most High a great King. What is He King over?

cards.text: Then the psalm turns from who this King is to what He does for His people. And it starts with the nations.

cards.question: True or false: the psalm says God subdues nations beneath His people.

cards.text: Next comes an inheritance, and an old name: Jacob, the father of Israel's twelve tribes (Genesis 49:28).

cards.question: True or false: the psalm says God's people pick out their own inheritance.
God chooses the inheritance, the pride of Jacob, whom He ___.

cards.text: Then comes a Selah. After it, God has ascended amid shouts of joy.

cards.question: God goes up amid shouts of joy. What sound goes up with Him?

cards.text: The next verse says sing praises FOUR times, to God and to our King. That's my oven timer when I pretend I didn't hear it the first three.

cards.question: After all those calls to sing praises, the psalm gives the reason. What is it?

answers.text: God is King of all the earth
God has sent rain on the land
God has ended the long famine

cards.text: Then the psalm says it plain: God reigns over the nations. This King does not clock out at five.

cards.question: True or false: the psalm pictures God seated on His holy throne.

cards.text: The last verse opens on a gathering: the nobles of the nations have assembled. That's a guest list where EVERY name comes with a title.

cards.question: The nobles of the nations assemble as the people of which God?

cards.text: That's Abraham, the man God told that all the families of the earth would be blessed through him (Genesis 12:3).

cards.question: The psalm says the shields of the earth belong to ___.

cards.text: And the psalm lands right here: He is highly exalted. I went from a 25 cent bin to my own bakery, so I know a little about getting lifted up, but friend, NOBODY gets lifted higher than Him.

findings.problem: The blank is the last word of Psalm 47:4 ('whom He ___'). The baker has to guess the line's wording ('loves' vs 'tests' or 'warns'). Nothing told so far lets them reason it out, which makes this the same pattern as the Psalm 23 bad example. A question about meaning would work better, such as what Psalm 47:4 says about how God feels toward Jacob.

rule.text: Never ask the baker to guess the next words of a line.

findings.problem: The story card is flat narration with none of Papa Dorin's voice: 'Next comes an inheritance, and an old name...' It reads as a plain note, not as him telling the psalm.

rule.text: Short, but not stripped down. A story card still has enough of Papa Dorin's voice and enough context that the moment makes sense.

findings.problem: 'Then comes a Selah. After it, God has ascended amid shouts of joy.' This is stripped down. It has no voice, and it gives little sense of the moment before the baker is asked about the sound of the horn.
